topic: the compliance line an MLS expects on a staged photo
angle: MLS and NAR rules ask a staged listing photo to say it was staged. Stagify applies that tag before the file leaves the studio, so forgetting it is not a thing the agent can do. The post shows the tag as a real pixel on a real render and spells out how little work it takes: one tick, four looks, a size slider.
visualSummary: One landscape render of a modern dining room on the deep blue field, marked with three numbered brand blue pins and a numbered legend beneath it. The room is a long oak table on a woven charcoal rug under a linear walnut pendant, black dining chairs with ivory boucle seats, a large abstract print in charcoal and cream on the far wall, and a window throwing daylight from the left. Pin one sits on the table top, pin two on the framed print, pin three on the floor beside the dark disclosure chip burnt into the bottom right of the photograph, which reads Virtually staged. A two tone headline sits above the photo and a white CTA pill in the footer.

copy.headline: You cannot forget the label.
copy.caption:
Every staged photo on an MLS has to say it was staged. Ours says it before you download it.

Here is the whole job:

1. Tick "Label as virtually staged" in the staging panel.
2. Pick the look. A dark chip, a light chip, text only, or a band across the foot of the photo.
3. Drag the size if you want it louder.

That is the feature. There is no step four.

The tag is burned into the file, not laid over the preview, so it survives the download, the email and the re upload. And if the tag cannot be applied, you do not get the image. That is on purpose. A photo you believe is labelled and is not is the exact problem the tag exists to prevent.

The dining room here is a real render. The table, the chairs, the rug, the pendant and the print were all generated. The room was empty. The tag in the corner went on by itself.

NAR Article 12 and most MLS rules ask for the same thing: if a listing photo has been altered, say so. Nobody is asking for an essay. Two words in the corner is enough.

First render is free, no card. Link in bio.

generation.modelNote: labelVirtuallyStaged is ON, which every other post in the history leaves off. The template chrome already carries the disclosure line, so a burnt-in badge normally says the same thing twice; here the badge IS the subject, and a post claiming the tag is applied for you while showing an unstamped render would prove the opposite of what it says. stampScale is 1.5 rather than the default 1.0: the badge is deliberately unobtrusive at 2% of the long edge, which is right on a listing photo and wrong on a frame asking the viewer to look at it after Instagram has compressed it. 1.5 is inside the product's own slider range of 0.7 to 1.6, so it is a configuration a customer can reach rather than a rendering path invented for the advertisement. Style stays `dark`, the default look. Rule 3 otherwise untouched: gemini-3.1-flash-image, full retry loop, never skipQualityReview, three attempts per photo across three different source photos.
generation.authorNote: Rule 4 applied: quality.perfect was false, so both candidate renders were opened at full size before anything was written, and the chair bases were checked specifically because they are the account's known artifact. On the kept render the automated reviewer's three complaints do not describe the delivered image: its two 80s were scored against the OTHER two attempts, and its 85 against this one is the cosmetic point that the chairs are not tucked in. At full zoom every chair in the frame carries four complete legs with correct joints, correct splay and contact shadows meeting the floor. The pins were then placed off the seating anyway, on the table, the print and the floor beside the badge, so the frame never invites inspection of the one element most likely to fail.

devilsAdvocate.whyThisOne: The only candidate that converts a liability into a reason to leave the feed. The previous eight posts sold capability, speed, breadth or price, all of which are pleasant to agree with and free to ignore. This one asks a question an agent cannot answer from the feed, namely whether the staged photos already on their active listings carry the disclosure their MLS wants, and the only way to resolve it is to go and look. The advocate stated explicitly that this is a reasoned argument rather than an evidenced one: none of the nine published posts has been measured, so nothing here rests on past performance.
devilsAdvocate.residualRisk: The badge is deliberately small, and pinning it makes it the subject. Under Instagram compression it either turns to illegible mush, which kills the proof, or reads as an intrusive watermark, which repels the agents it should reassure. Answered rather than accepted: stampScale 1.5 puts the tag at about 3% of the long edge instead of 2%, which is legible at feed size and still visibly a corner chip rather than a band across the photo. The `banner` style, which is the intrusive one, was available and not used.
devilsAdvocate.userDirection: The user picked i10 over the two runners up and asked that the frame outline how easy the labelling actually is. That moved the argument from pure risk to risk plus effort: the legend now ends on the tag going on for you, and the caption is a three step list with an explicit note that there is no step four.
